children: Japanese households have poured record sums into 5-year fixed-rate government bonds, signalling expectations that domestic bond yields are peaking.

The surge in Japanese government bond yields to multi-decade highs last month has made households increasingly sensitive to investment returns. That's prompted some to shift a portion of the $7 trillion they hold in low-interest bank deposits into so-called retail JGBs.
Sales of retail JGBs have reached 8.19 trillion yen ($51.77 billion) so far this fiscal year, already surpassing the previous full-year record of 7.27 trillion yen set in fiscal 2005.

Issuance for November doubled from October to 2.03 trillion yen, Finance Ministry data released on Friday showed, with 5-year fixed-rate bonds making up 65% of the total, while 10-year floating-rate notes accounted for just 18%.

"Fewer people appear to anticipate further upside to rates," said Katsutoshi Inadome, senior strategist at Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Asset Management. "The prevailing sentiment seems to be that 5-year fixed is sufficient."

The appeal of 5-year bonds has also been reinforced by a widening coupon advantage. The November issue carries a 2.39% coupon on 5-year fixed bonds, compared with 2.05% on 10-year floating-rate notes, a 0.34 percentage point premium and the widest since July 2007. December coupons are set at 2.17% and 1.85%, respectively.

The Bank of Japan in October declared victory in its battle to lift inflation to 2% and is widely expected to raise its key rate to 1.5% in December. A Reuters poll of analysts showed they expect further increases towards a terminal rate of around 1.75% to 2.0%.

"With 5-year fixed yields closing in on the terminal rate priced in by markets, investors may have decided that locking in at current levels is more advantageous," said Rinto Maruyama, strategist at SMBC Nikko Securities.
